lectures.title: Monitoring System Activity: the `htop` Program (Alternative to `top`)

cues.en: Let's now have a look at the program top you might have heard me before referring to that program.
So let's have a look at that.
It's an easier to use alternative to top and it's available on most Linux systems, but we might have
to install it as an additional software.
So we might we have to be allowed from our company, for example, to allow additional software and
it should also be available in the default repositories.
And for some Linux systems it may not be available or it may be really, really complicated to install
it and then we might not want to install it.
But on most Linux systems this is available.
So for example on Ubuntu we could install it with an apt get install H top and then we would install
that program.
So let's have a look at this.
So here first I need or if I just try to start that program, you can see here that we need to install
it so I can say sudo apt or apt get it doesn't matter, install h top and then the program will be installed.
Of course I have to provide my password here and you can see it's not really big, but we need to install
it.
By the way on centos a simple sudo dnf install h top here is enough.
Then I just need to enter my password and then we can see here that I am now being offered to install
h top.
The only thing is it's coming from the extra packages for enterprise Linux.
But on my system I have them enabled so I can just confirm with the Y and now H top is installed.
So I'm now switching back to my ubuntu.
Now I can launch it and depending on my system configuration, if I give myself admin rights or root
rights when I start the program, I do.
I can see all of the processes.
It's again the same restriction as with the top program.
It's trying to access um, virtual files from the slash proc directory.
And some of those files can only be accessed with root privileges.
So I put a pseudo in front so that we can see everything here.
You can see a big advantage here that we get a really nice overview and that also the colors are really,
really nice.
Here.
You can see here a list of our CPU cores.
So here we have two CPUs in that system.
It's virtual CPUs.
So if one CPU is shown as like two or for example as two CPUs to our system, then it would show those
two CPUs.
So it's those virtual cores that are displayed here.
With the current usage, we see the load average.
So the how many CPU cores we have used in the last one minute in the last five minutes and in the last
15 minutes we see the uptime, how long our system is running already.
And we can also see here, for example, the amount of memory that we are using and the amount of swap.
Um, how do we navigate this one here so we can navigate with our arrow keys, we can scroll or go down
or up, or you can also see that the list is scrollable.
So that's really, really useful.
But we can also, for example, navigate to the right if we want to see the whole command that is displayed
here, the next thing we can use, but only if our shell supports this.
It's like a combination of the program must support it, but also our shell must support it.
That it sends this to our program.
But you can see here, I'm also able to click on those columns, for example, to change the order or
to order by another column.
So you can imagine that this is extremely useful and it's way more convenient than going through a lot
of menus.
We have a lot of other options here though, at as well.
So, for example, if I would want to change the niceness of a process, I could just hit the F8 key
to change the niceness here And now you can see here that I'm now increasing the niceness of that process.
Uh, it has refreshed and then the position was different.
But if I hit F8, you can see here that the niceness is being increased.
But I need to be really, really careful because I'm always at the third position here.
But you can see how the actual process that I'm referring to is changing.
If I want to decrease the niceness, I could use the F7 key.
And there you see it written here that this will decrease the niceness.
So you can see here I can navigate to my process and then decrease the niceness.
Just be aware it might require root privileges.
So you might have had to start up with root privileges.
So you can imagine that this is also really, really convenient.
Another way that we can use here is the F9 key.
For example, to kill a program.
This doesn't kill a program, but we get a selection of which kind of signal we want to send to this
program.
We also see that this program stays highlighted here, and now we can choose which signal we want.
We don't need to remember those.
We don't need to enter those.
But we could also, for example, just cancel that either by selecting, cancel or by pressing the escape
key.
So this is also really convenient here.
Another way that we can also use is that we can enter the F5 key and then you can see that all the processes
are being displayed here as a tree.
And you can also imagine that this can be useful.
We can see which process has launched, which other process.
So yeah, and we can also untoggle that one again by just pressing F5 again.
The next thing we can do is that we can also, for example, with the F2 key, we can go into more advanced
option menu.
And now, for example, we could change the meters.
So for example, here right now, as a memory display, we have a bar, but for example, we could enter
here and then we could, for example, move it around and then hit enter again to store it at that place.
But we could also, for example, change the style by pressing the space key.
And there, for example, we could have a short, a small graph or we could have it as Led symbols or
just as a bar.
We could also here add additional meters.
So for example, if we would like to show the current time, I could just hit go with the arrow keys
to clock here, hit enter.
And now, for example, I could move it here to this column or to this column and then hit enter to
confirm this.
And now you can see that it's also showing my current time.
I can also do more, though, for example, here you can see here I can go into the setup column and
then, for example, I could switch to display options and then you can see how many different options
I have here.
So for example, here the CPUs start count at the zero, but I could say they should start counting
at the one so you can see how many different options we got here.
And we could also, for example, show the frequency of the CPU.
It doesn't work on my system or the temperature, which I think also doesn't work on my system because
this is a virtual machine that's running on a mac and it doesn't seem to be working here.
But on a real server, this, for example, would work or should usually work.
And you can imagine that this can be really convenient.
Or we could also change the colors or add additional columns so we can really customize the output here.
If we are ready, we can just hit the F10 key.
It's showing us that again here at the lower at the bottom of our screen.
And then I would hit F10 and now you can see here, this is now well I haven't changed that much, but
I've changed that.
The time will be shown here.
The next thing I could do is either if I want to, if I want to forget about my changes, I could just
quit that program with control C If I send this interrupt signal, then it's just being quit.
But if I want to save it on the configuration that I did, I need to press the F10 key and this is a
normal quit of that program.
It's supported by that program.
It's completely implemented by stop.
And if I press F10, it's quitting but also storing that configuration.
So if I now would launch it again, you can see here the time is still being shown.
Of course it's the same as with top.
It has a different configuration depending on which user is executing that program.
So here, for example, pseudo stop has a different configuration because this means that this program
is being run as the root user and this is being run as the normal user.
So you can see that whenever you have this program available, this can be way more convenient than
the top program and especially because of this bar at the lower end of the screen, you don't have to
learn that much.
You can really just it's more self-explanatory.
And I would recommend you to use this one whenever you're able to install additional software and you're
able to easily install that tool.
All right.
This much about the top command.
